title: How Much Does Spray Foam Insulation Cost in St. George, Utah? (2026 Guide)
metaTitle: Spray Foam Cost St. George, UT (2026) | St. George Foam
metaDescription: 2026 spray foam insulation pricing for St. George, UT homes: open-cell vs closed-cell cost drivers, project examples, and how to get an accurate quote.
author: St. George Foam Team
excerpt: Spray foam pricing in Washington County generally runs $1.50 to $5.00 per square foot, but the number that actually matters is what drives your specific project up or down that range. Here's how the estimate actually gets built.
content: The honest answer to "how much does spray foam cost" is a range, not a number: roughly $1.50 to $5.00 per square foot installed across Washington County, with open-cell foam sitting at the lower end and closed-cell at the higher end. That's a wide enough range that it isn't very useful on its own, so this guide walks through what actually pushes a specific project toward one end or the other.

Open-cell versus closed-cell is the biggest single driver. Open-cell runs cheaper per square foot because it's a lighter-density product that expands more per unit of material, so it costs less to fill the same cavity. Closed-cell is priced by the board-foot at a higher rate because it's denser, cures to roughly double the R-value per inch, and resists moisture in a way open-cell doesn't. A whole-attic open-cell job and a roof-deck closed-cell conversion on the same size house can land at meaningfully different total costs, and that's before either number gets adjusted for access or thickness.

Project type is the second driver. New construction, where framing is open and there's no old insulation to deal with, is generally the most efficient install condition and prices accordingly. Retrofit and remodel work costs more per square foot when it involves removing damaged fiberglass first, working around finished surfaces, or coordinating around occupied space. A correction job -- removing a previous contractor's failed foam before re-spraying -- has its own separate cost structure entirely, since removal, disposal, and substrate inspection all get added before the new foam goes in.

Square footage and application type matter more than most homeowners expect. A 2,000 square foot attic floor seal and a 2,000 square foot roof-deck conversion on the same house are not the same price, because the roof-deck job usually runs thicker closed-cell foam across a larger, more complex surface -- rafter bays, ridge details, eave transitions -- while an attic floor seal is a flatter, more straightforward plane. Crawl space and rim joist work is priced by linear footage of perimeter wall rather than a flat square-foot number, since crawl space height and access change the labor time more than the square footage alone does.

Access is the factor that surprises people most. A full-height, walkable attic with a generous hatch costs less to work in than a low-clearance tile-roof attic where the crew is working on their knees the whole time. A detached shop with open truss framing installs faster than an attached garage ceiling with existing drywall that has to come down first. We measure and photograph the actual space during every estimate specifically because access differences like this can move a quote meaningfully in either direction.

Commercial and metal building pricing works a little differently. Those jobs are quoted by total interior panel square footage -- roof and walls typically priced separately since roof access usually requires lift equipment -- and by the target thickness for the building's actual use case. A basic condensation-control pass on an ag building costs less per square foot than a full climate-controlled shop insulation package, even on buildings of similar size.

A few real-world reference points help make the range concrete. A typical 1,800 to 2,200 square foot St. George home getting an attic-floor open-cell seal usually lands toward the lower-middle of the range on a per-square-foot basis. The same home converting to a full closed-cell roof-deck system costs more overall, both because closed-cell runs a higher rate and because the roof deck surface area, including rafter bays and transitions, is larger than the flat attic floor. A two-car attached garage ceiling insulation project is a smaller total dollar figure but can carry a higher per-square-foot rate if drywall removal is part of the scope. A mid-size metal shop or self-storage building runs into a different pricing conversation entirely, driven by total panel area and lift access rather than a simple square-foot multiplier.

Rocky Mountain Power's Wattsmart Homes program is worth checking before you finalize a project, since it periodically offers rebates tied to qualifying insulation and air-sealing upgrades for customers in its service territory. Dixie Power customers should ask their provider directly about any current efficiency incentive, since program availability changes. Either way, it's worth factoring a potential rebate into your net cost conversation before assuming the sticker price is the final number.

The way to get an accurate number for your specific project is an on-site estimate, not a phone quote based on square footage alone. We walk the attic, crawl space, garage, or building in question, measure the actual area, check access and existing insulation condition, and build the number from what's actually there rather than a generic per-square-foot average. Call 844-967-5247 or email josh@contractorschoiceagency.com to schedule a walkthrough, and we'll leave you with a written scope and price before any work starts.

Timing your project also has a real effect on scheduling, if not always directly on price. Spring and early summer -- before June's heat and well before the mid-July monsoon window -- tends to be the busiest stretch for attic and roof-deck work in Washington County, since homeowners are trying to get ahead of peak cooling season. Booking a few weeks out from that rush, either earlier in spring or in the fall after monsoon season winds down in September, generally means more scheduling flexibility and less pressure to compress a multi-day commercial job into a tight window.

One more factor worth planning for: disposal and prep costs on correction or retrofit jobs. If your project involves removing old, damaged, or previously failed insulation before new foam goes in, that removal and haul-off is a real line item, not a rounding error, and it's part of why a correction project (see our spray foam removal and correction service) is priced separately from a straightforward new install. Ask for that breakdown explicitly if your project involves any removal, so you're comparing quotes on an apples-to-apples basis rather than one contractor quietly skipping a step another one included.

faqs.q: Is closed-cell always worth the higher price over open-cell?
faqs.a: Not always -- it depends on the application. Closed-cell earns its higher cost on roof decks, crawl space walls, and exterior-exposed surfaces where moisture resistance and rigidity matter. On interior partition walls or a vented attic floor, open-cell often delivers the comfort improvement you're after at a lower total cost.

faqs.q: Does removing old insulation before spraying cost extra?
faqs.a: Yes, when it's necessary -- removing sagging, damaged, or rodent-contaminated fiberglass adds a labor step before the foam goes in. We'll tell you during the walkthrough whether your existing insulation needs to come out first or whether we can spray without removing it.

faqs.q: Can I get a rough price over the phone before an on-site visit?
faqs.a: We can give you a general range based on square footage and project type, but the firm number always comes from an on-site walkthrough, since access, existing insulation condition, and roof or building specifics can move the price meaningfully in either direction.

title: 5 Signs Your Spray Foam Job Was Installed Wrong (And What to Do About It)
metaTitle: Signs of a Bad Spray Foam Job | St. George Foam
metaDescription: How to spot a failed or off-ratio spray foam install in your St. George home -- odor, texture, gaps, and inspection issues -- and what correction involves.
author: St. George Foam Team
excerpt: Spray foam is a two-part chemical reaction happening live in your attic or crawl space, and when the ratio or technique is off, the failure shows up in predictable, recognizable ways. Here's what to look for.
content: Spray foam insulation is a chemical reaction, not a material that's simply applied -- an A-side and a B-side component are pumped through heated hoses at a precise ratio and mixed at the gun tip, curing into a stable foam structure within seconds of hitting the surface. When that ratio, temperature, or technique is off, the result isn't invisible. It shows up as a specific set of symptoms that a homeowner can usually spot without needing to be an insulation expert, and knowing what they are is the first step to getting it fixed.

Sign one is a smell that won't quit. A correctly cured spray foam job has a noticeable chemical odor for the first day or two after installation, which is normal and expected as the last of the reaction finishes off-gassing. If that smell is still strong a week later, and especially if it's still noticeable a month or more later, that's a strong indicator the foam is off-ratio and never fully cured. Off-ratio foam can continue releasing uncured chemical compounds indefinitely because the reaction that's supposed to lock them into a stable structure never finished.

Sign two is texture. Reach up and press on the foam in an accessible spot -- an attic rafter bay or an exposed rim joist, for example. Correctly cured foam is firm: open-cell has some give but springs back, closed-cell is rigid. Foam that stays tacky or soft to the touch, feels spongy in a way that doesn't spring back, or crumbles and flakes apart when pressed is showing the physical signature of an off-ratio mix or a botched cure.

Sign three is visible gaps and thin spots, especially in the places that are hardest to spray evenly -- tight eave lines, rim joist corners, and around obstructions like plumbing stacks or electrical boxes. A rushed job, or a technician working in a space with limited access, often skips or shorts these transition areas even when the flat, easy-to-reach surfaces look fine. A quick visual check with a flashlight at the eaves and corners of an attic often tells you more than checking the wide-open middle of the roof deck.

Sign four is foam pulling away from what it was sprayed onto -- delaminating from roof decking, wall framing, or a metal panel, sometimes visible as a hairline gap or a section that's clearly no longer bonded. This can happen from an off-ratio mix that never achieved proper adhesion, from spraying over a dirty or contaminated surface, or in some cases from moisture that got trapped behind the foam and worked it loose over time.

Sign five is a failed inspection tied specifically to the foam -- most commonly a missing ignition-barrier or thermal-barrier coating over foam that's exposed to living or storage space rather than sealed behind drywall. This is a code requirement, not an optional finish, and it's one of the more common things we find missing when we're called in after an inspector flags a job. It's also one of the easiest things for a rushed installer to skip, since it's an extra coating pass after the foam itself is already sprayed and, to an untrained eye, the job already looks finished.

If you're recognizing one or more of these signs, the next step is an on-site assessment rather than guessing. We check cure state, coverage, and thickness across the whole assembly -- not just the spot you noticed the problem -- because off-ratio mixing from a miscalibrated rig or an inconsistent technician often affects more of the job than the one section that first caught your attention.

Correction almost never means starting completely over. In most cases we remove only the sections that actually failed -- mechanically scraping and cutting the bad foam away from the roof decking, framing, or panel underneath rather than chemically dissolving it, which protects the structure from further damage -- and re-spray those areas with the correct product, ratio, and thickness. Where a missing ignition barrier is the only issue, sometimes the fix is simply adding the required coating rather than removing any foam at all.

This kind of work comes up more often than people expect, for a few consistent reasons: rushed timelines on production-home schedules, a technician who's newer and hasn't caught a drifting ratio mid-job, spray equipment that wasn't properly calibrated or maintained that day, or a crew working in weather conditions -- too hot, too cold, wrong humidity -- outside the product's application range without adjusting technique for it. None of those are things a homeowner can see happening in real time, which is exactly why the after-the-fact signs above matter.

If you're seeing one or more of these signs, resist the urge to handle it yourself before getting a professional assessment. Cutting into or disturbing off-ratio foam without knowing the extent of the problem can spread loose material, expose you to uncured chemical compounds unnecessarily, or mask evidence an inspector or a correction crew would otherwise use to diagnose the root cause. Instead, photograph what you're seeing -- the texture, any visible gaps, the specific locations -- and note when the smell or issue was first noticed, since that timeline is genuinely useful information during the diagnostic walkthrough.

It's also worth acting on this sooner rather than later, particularly for roof-deck or crawl space applications. Foam that's disbonded from decking or framing, or that trapped moisture behind it during a botched application, can allow ongoing moisture exposure to the wood underneath even after the immediate odor or texture issue seems to have settled down. The earlier a correction crew can assess and address it, the less likely the underlying structure has taken on additional damage in the meantime.

faqs.q: Is it normal for spray foam to smell strong for the first few days?
faqs.a: Yes -- a noticeable chemical smell for the first day or two after installation is expected as the final part of the cure finishes off-gassing. It's a smell persisting well beyond that window that points to a problem, not the initial smell itself.

faqs.q: Can I press on my attic's spray foam myself to check it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you can safely access it -- press firmly on an exposed section and see whether it feels firm and stable or soft, tacky, and spongy. It's a reasonable first check, though an on-site professional assessment is the way to confirm what you're feeling.

faqs.q: Does a bad spray foam job always mean a full removal?
faqs.a: No -- most correction jobs address only the sections that actually failed rather than the entire installation. We assess coverage and cure state across the whole assembly before recommending removal, and we only remove what's actually necessary.

faqs.q: What if the company that did the original install won't fix it?
faqs.a: We take on correction work regardless of who did the original install, including situations where the original contractor is unresponsive, out of business, or disputing the problem. We'll assess it independently and give you a clear, documented scope either way.

title: Why Metal Buildings in St. George Sweat -- and How Spray Foam Stops It
metaTitle: Metal Building Condensation Fix | St. George Foam
metaDescription: Why metal buildings, pole barns & warehouses in the St. George desert climate condensate, and how direct-to-metal spray foam solves it. Call 844-967-5247.
author: St. George Foam Team
excerpt: A metal roof in a 106-degree desert can still drip condensation by sunrise. It's not a defect -- it's basic physics colliding with an uninsulated steel panel, and it has a specific, well-understood fix.
content: It surprises a lot of building owners the first time they see it: a metal roof panel, baked all day in 104 to 106-degree July heat, dripping water onto stored inventory by early morning. It looks like a roof leak, but there's often no leak at all -- it's condensation, and it's a predictable, physics-driven problem in exactly the kind of desert climate St. George sits in.

The mechanism is straightforward once you see it laid out. Metal panels have almost no thermal mass, so their surface temperature tracks the surrounding air almost instantly, with no lag the way a thick masonry or wood-framed wall has. St. George's dry desert air means clear skies most nights, and clear skies allow strong radiant cooling -- exposed surfaces radiate heat out to the night sky faster than they absorb it back from the surrounding air, so a metal roof panel can end up colder than the ambient outdoor air temperature by early morning. If that panel surface drops below the interior dew point -- which depends on how much moisture is inside the building from vehicles, livestock, stored materials, or simple occupancy -- water condenses directly on the steel.

This is a bigger issue here than it sounds like it should be, precisely because the desert climate has such a wide day-to-night temperature swing. A summer day pushing past 104 degrees can still see a night-time low back in the 70s, and that swing is exactly what drives strong radiant cooling of an exposed metal surface after sunset. Buildings in more moderate, humid climates with smaller diurnal swings don't see the same intensity of overnight condensation, even though people assume a wetter climate would be the bigger risk.

The consequences compound over time. Dripping condensation onto stored hay, feed, or agricultural product causes direct spoilage. On stored vehicles, RVs, or boats, it's a slow path to corrosion and interior mildew. On tools, inventory, or equipment in a shop or warehouse, it's rust and degraded packaging. And on the building's own steel framing -- the purlins and structural members behind the panel -- years of repeated condensation cycling is a genuine long-term corrosion risk to the structure itself, not just what's stored inside it.

The traditional fix in a lot of pole barn and ag building construction is a fiberglass blanket system stapled or screwed up against the underside of the panel, sometimes with a separate vapor-barrier facing. It helps, but it has a structural weakness: the blanket relies on staying tightly compressed against the panel to work, and over time it sags, gaps open at the seams and screw penetrations, and once a gap opens, humid interior air reaches the cold steel behind the insulation and condenses right there -- often invisibly, inside the wall or roof assembly, until it's caused enough damage to notice from the outside.

Spray foam solves the actual mechanism, not just the symptom. Closed-cell foam sprayed directly onto the interior face of the metal panel bonds to the steel with no air gap at all -- there's no cavity for humid air to migrate into and reach a cold surface, because the insulation is the surface it's touching. That direct adhesion is the real reason spray foam stops metal building condensation more reliably than a blanket system: it removes the physical pathway the moisture needs, not just adds R-value.

There's a secondary benefit building owners notice immediately even before the condensation issue fully proves itself out over a season: noise. An uninsulated metal roof turns a monsoon downpour or hailstorm into a genuinely loud event inside the building. A few inches of closed-cell foam sprayed to the roof panel measurably dampens that noise, which matters for anything from a working shop to an event space to livestock that get stressed by loud weather.

This work applies across a wide range of building types around Washington County -- self-storage facilities protecting customers' stored belongings, RV and boat storage buildings, agricultural and ranch buildings, steel-frame shops and light-industrial space, and pole barns of every size. If you're seeing unexplained moisture on the inside of a metal roof or wall panel, especially first thing in the morning after a hot, clear day, condensation -- not a roof leak -- is the first thing worth ruling in or out before assuming you need a roofer.

It's worth framing the cost of fixing this against what condensation actually puts at risk. A self-storage operator with customer belongings on the line, a rancher with feed or equipment stored under a metal roof, or a shop owner with inventory and tools exposed to overnight drip damage is weighing a one-time insulation cost against a recurring, compounding loss that shows up as spoiled product, corroded tools, or customer complaints. Framed that way, the spray foam project is usually closer to a maintenance investment than a discretionary upgrade.

We also get asked whether ventilation alone -- ridge vents, powered exhaust fans, or simply leaving doors open -- can solve the problem instead of insulation. Ventilation can reduce interior humidity somewhat, which helps at the margins, but it doesn't change the underlying physics of a bare metal panel radiating below the dew point on a clear night. In most cases we see, buildings already running ventilation still condensate, because moving air around the space doesn't stop the panel surface itself from getting cold enough to trigger it. Direct-to-metal insulation addresses the actual surface temperature problem instead of just managing the humidity around it.

faqs.q: How do I know if it's condensation and not an actual roof leak?
faqs.a: Condensation typically shows up as widespread moisture across the underside of the panel, often worse near sunrise after a clear night, rather than a localized drip tied to a specific seam, fastener, or penetration. A physical inspection of the panel and any suspect leak points is the reliable way to tell the two apart.

faqs.q: Will spray foam completely eliminate condensation, or just reduce it?
faqs.a: When applied correctly with full coverage and adequate thickness, direct-to-metal closed-cell foam effectively eliminates the condensation mechanism, since it removes the air gap and vapor pathway that lets interior humidity reach the cold steel surface.

faqs.q: Does this work on an existing metal building, or only new construction?
faqs.a: It works on existing buildings just as well as new ones -- most of our commercial and metal building work is retrofitting insulation into buildings that were built with none, or replacing a failed fiberglass blanket system.

faqs.q: How thick does the foam need to be to stop condensation?
faqs.a: It depends on the building's use case -- a basic condensation-control pass runs thinner than a full climate-controlled shop insulation package. We size it during the on-site assessment based on what the building is actually being used for.

title: Open-Cell vs. Closed-Cell Spray Foam: Which One Does Your Washington County Home Need?
metaTitle: Open-Cell vs Closed-Cell Foam St. George | St. George Foam
metaDescription: Practical open-cell vs closed-cell spray foam comparison for St. George, UT homes -- R-value, cost, moisture, and where each one actually belongs.
author: St. George Foam Team
excerpt: The two products aren't competing for the same job -- they're built for different parts of the house. Here's a practical, room-by-room way to think about which one belongs where.
content: Homeowners researching spray foam usually start by asking which is "better," open-cell or closed-cell, as if one is simply the upgraded version of the other. That's not really how the decision works. They're different products built for different conditions, and the right answer is almost always "both, in different parts of the house" rather than picking one for the entire project.

It helps to think of the two products less like a good-versus-better pair and more like two different tools in the same toolbox -- a framing hammer and a finish hammer both drive nails, but you wouldn't reach for the same one on every job. Open-cell and closed-cell both insulate and both air-seal, but they're formulated around different priorities, and a contractor who understands both will end up specifying different products on different walls of the same house without that being a contradiction.

Start with the numbers, because they explain most of the rest of the decision. Open-cell cures to roughly R-3.5 to R-3.7 per inch. Closed-cell cures to roughly R-6 to R-7 per inch -- close to double. That difference exists because closed-cell has a much denser cell structure, packed with an insulating gas rather than open air pockets, and that density is also what gives closed-cell its resistance to moisture and its added rigidity. Open-cell's more open structure is lighter, expands more per unit of material, and costs less installed as a result, generally toward the $1.50 to $2.50 per square foot range versus closed-cell trending higher, often into the $3.00 to $5.00 range depending on thickness and access.

Moisture behavior is the part that actually matters most for deciding where each one goes. Closed-cell is highly resistant to bulk water and largely impermeable to water vapor, which makes it the right call anywhere it's exposed to real moisture risk -- a roof deck exposed to the outside, a crawl space perimeter wall a few inches off graded soil, a rim joist sitting right at the transition between conditioned and unconditioned space, or a metal building panel prone to condensation. Open-cell doesn't have that resistance, and using it in any of those locations risks trapping moisture against wood framing or decking rather than shedding it.

In St. George's dry desert climate, that moisture concern is smaller than it would be in a humid region, but it doesn't disappear -- the mid-July through early-to-mid-September monsoon window brings real rain events, and a roof deck or crawl space wall still needs to handle occasional bulk moisture exposure regardless of how dry the rest of the year is. That's why the application, not the general climate, is what drives the open-cell versus closed-cell call.

Cost-per-R-point is another way to compare the two that homeowners sometimes overlook. Because closed-cell delivers roughly double the R-value per inch, a thinner layer of closed-cell can match or exceed the R-value of a much thicker open-cell fill in the same cavity -- which matters in a shallow 2x4 wall where there simply isn't much depth to work with. In a deep attic floor joist bay with plenty of room, that advantage matters less, since open-cell has the depth available to reach a strong whole-assembly R-value on its own without needing closed-cell's per-inch efficiency.

Structural rigidity is the other factor that tips decisions toward closed-cell in specific spots. A few inches of closed-cell foam sprayed into a wall or roof assembly adds real stiffness on top of what the framing alone provides -- which is part of why it's the standard product for metal buildings and pole barns, where it's contributing structurally to the panel system, not just insulating it.

Sound control is open-cell's clearest practical win, and it's one homeowners notice immediately in a way they never notice R-value. Its softer, more open structure absorbs sound transmission through a wall noticeably better than a rigid closed-cell fill, which is why interior partition walls -- between a primary suite and a laundry room, around a home office, between bedrooms -- are a place we default to open-cell even on a project that's using closed-cell everywhere else.

Put together in a practical, room-by-room way: closed-cell belongs at the roof deck, crawl space perimeter walls, rim joists, and anywhere spraying against metal panel construction. Open-cell belongs in interior partition walls, attic floors in homes keeping a traditional vented attic, and any interior cavity where air-sealing and cost efficiency matter more than moisture resistance or added rigidity. Exterior walls can go either way depending on cavity depth, budget, and how much of that wall is exposed to real weather versus sheltered behind stucco or siding with a drainage plane doing some of the work already.

Most whole-house or whole-property projects we run end up using both products on the same job -- closed-cell where moisture and rigidity matter, open-cell where cost efficiency and sound control matter -- sprayed by the same crew in the same visit rather than treating it as an either-or decision made once at the start of the project.

If you're getting quotes and a contractor recommends one product for the entire house without walking through which surfaces are exposed to moisture, which are load-bearing or structural, and which are purely interior, that's worth a follow-up question. A single-product recommendation for a whole house isn't automatically wrong, but it should come with a specific reason tied to your home's actual layout, not just a default answer the contractor gives everyone. Ask directly: why closed-cell here and not open-cell, or vice versa, for this specific wall or ceiling? A contractor who's actually assessed your home should have a concrete answer for each area, not a one-size-fits-all pitch.

faqs.q: Can I just use closed-cell everywhere to get the best of both?
faqs.a: You could, but it usually isn't worth the added cost in applications where closed-cell's specific advantages -- moisture resistance and rigidity -- aren't actually needed, like an interior partition wall. Matching the product to the application gets you better value than defaulting to the more expensive option everywhere.

faqs.q: Which one is better for soundproofing a home office or bedroom?
faqs.a: Open-cell, consistently. Its softer, more open cell structure absorbs interior sound transmission noticeably better than closed-cell's rigid fill, which is why it's the default choice for interior partition walls even on jobs using closed-cell elsewhere.

faqs.q: Is open-cell a bad choice in our monsoon season?
faqs.a: Not for its intended applications -- interior walls and vented attic floors. The concern with open-cell and moisture applies to direct exposure locations like roof decks and crawl space walls, which is exactly why those get closed-cell instead, regardless of how short or long the monsoon window is in a given year.

faqs.q: Does closed-cell really add structural strength, or is that marketing?
faqs.a: It's a real, measurable effect -- a few inches of cured closed-cell foam bonded into a wall or roof assembly adds stiffness beyond the framing alone, which is a documented part of why it's the standard product for metal building and pole barn wall systems.
